Algorithm studio

Edit an implementation, then benchmark it on your device.

BUILT-IN IMPLEMENTATIONJavaScript · sort(input) → number[]
ANSI C89 · compiled on your device

Implement void sort(double input[], int n) and sort in place. Use /* comments */ and declare variables before statements. Standard headers such as <stdlib.h> are available. No main() is needed.

First use downloads about 19 MB of compiler files. Timings measure optimized WebAssembly (-O2), with compilation and input copying excluded. Console output is discarded during benchmarks.

Return a sorted array, or sort the input in place. Each timed run receives a fresh copy.

Measure fairly. Interpret carefully.
BenchMarker compares sorting implementations on identical inputs, using a dedicated worker so your experiment does not freeze the interface.
Actual running time
Each algorithm gets one untimed warm-up per case and fresh input copies for every repetition. The timer covers only the algorithm call. Results are checked against a correctly sorted reference, including every duplicate value. Charts use median milliseconds across repetitions.
ANSI C mode
Clang compiles ANSI C89 to WebAssembly on your device with -O2 optimization. Compiler loading, compilation, module instantiation, and input copying are excluded from timings. C and JavaScript have separate source drafts. CSV exports identify the language, compiler, and flags. These are browser WebAssembly timings, not native desktop C timings.
Theoretical growth
Big O describes how work grows, not a time in milliseconds. The dashed reference curve is scaled to your measured values using a least-squares coefficient. Theory shown is the usual average case for the built-in code; an edit can change it.
Empirical complexity
We fit constant, logarithmic, linear, n log n, quadratic, and cubic curves to observed medians. The best fit is descriptive, not proof of asymptotic complexity. Small inputs, JIT compilation, garbage collection, and other browser activity add noise.
Reproducibility
Generated experiments use a seeded input generator and five input sizes. Algorithms receive the same data at each size; their run order rotates across cases. Each algorithm/case has a 12-second limit. Exports include individual timings, configuration, device context, input fingerprints, source code, and validation status. Results remain in memory for this page session.
